items.title: Hybrid Machine Learning & Financial Econometrics: Building Volatility-Aware Dynamic Forecast Bands for Bitcoin
items.author: Selcuk Disci
items.description:

Continue reading: Hybrid Machine Learning & Financial Econometrics: Building Volatility-Aware Dynamic Forecast Bands for Bitcoin
items.content:
[This article was first published on DataGeeek, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here)
Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

When forecasting high-volatility financial assets like Bitcoin (BTC-USD), standard point-prediction models—whether classical ARIMA or deep neural networks—often fall short. A point estimate tells you where the model expects the price to go, but it completely ignores market regime shifts and changing risk levels.

In this article, we construct an end-to-end forecasting pipeline in R that combines Machine Learning (Multi-Layer Perceptron via brulee and tidymodels) for directional trend prediction with Financial Econometrics (GJR-GARCH via rugarch) to generate dynamic, volatility-adjusted confidence bounds.

The Architecture Overview

Instead of attempting to forecast level prices directly—which introduces non-stationarity issues—our pipeline operates on log returns and reconstructs price trajectories dynamically.

Key Architectural Decisions & Methodological Rationale

1. Modeling Log Returns Instead of Level Prices

Directly predicting raw prices often creates spurious regression results because price series are non-stationary. By transforming the price series to log returns:

rt=ln⁡(PtPt−1)r_t = \ln\left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}}\right)

This transformation achieves stationarity, making the target variable suitable for neural network training. Factual price predictions are reconstructed at test time via cumulative exponentiation:

P^t=Pt−1×exp⁡(r^t)\hat{P}_t = P_{t-1} \times \exp(\hat{r}_t)

2. Deep Learning for Trend: Multi-Layer Perceptron (brulee)

We use a 2-layer MLP architecture (32, 16) initialized via the tidymodels framework.

  • Lag Features: We supply 20 days of lagged log returns to capture short- to medium-term autocorrelation.
  • Normalizations & Dropping Zero Variance: Handled within a clean recipes pipeline to prevent data leakage

3. Econometric Volatility Modeling: GJR-GARCH(1,1) on Neural Network Residuals

Machine learning models capture the conditional mean, but their residuals, ϵt=rt−r^t \epsilon_t = r_t – \hat{r}_t , still contain volatility clustering—periods of high turbulence followed by high turbulence, and calm periods followed by calm.

To model this conditional variance (σt2\sigma_t^2), we fit a GJR-GARCH(1,1) model on the MLP training residuals:

σt2=ω+αϵt−12+γIt−1ϵt−12+βσt−12\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha \epsilon_{t-1}^2 + \gamma I_{t-1} \epsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta \sigma_{t-1}^2
  • Why GJR-GARCH over Standard GARCH? Crypto markets exhibit leverage effects: price drops often spark higher panic volatility than equivalent price rallies. The indicator term It−1I_{t-1} captures this asymmetry (γ\gamma).
  • Why garchOrder = c(1, 1)? The order (1,1) specifies a single lag for the ARCH component (ϵt−12\epsilon_{t-1}^2) and a single lag for the GARCH component (σt−12\sigma_{t-1}^2). Empirical literature demonstrates that a single lag captures the vast majority of volatility persistence without overfitting.
  • Why Skewed Student-t (sstd) Distribution? Bitcoin returns violate Gaussian normal distribution assumptions. They display fat tails (extreme events occur frequently) and skewness (asymmetric distribution). The sstd distribution explicitly models both heavy tails and skewness.
  • Solver Selection: We use solver = "hybrid" in rugarch to combine optimization algorithms, ensuring convergence even under complex distribution parameters.
Upper Boundt=P^t×exp⁡(+1.96×σt)\text{Upper Bound}_t = \hat{P}_t \times \exp(+1.96 \times \sigma_t)
Lower Boundt=P^t×exp⁡(−1.96×σt)\text{Lower Bound}_t = \hat{P}_t \times \exp(-1.96 \times \sigma_t)

When the market is quiet, these confidence bounds contract automatically. During volatile regimes, the bounds expand, giving a realistic probabilistic envelope rather than static, uninformative confidence intervals.

Complete R Implementation

Below is the complete, self-contained R script implementing the full pipeline using tidymodels, brulee, rugarch, and plotly.

# Integrated Forecasting Pipeline with tidymodels, yardstick, and plotly
library(tidymodels)
library(timetk)
library(brulee)
library(modeltime)
library(tidyquant)
library(plotly)
library(scales)
library(glue)
library(ggtext)
library(rugarch) # Added for GJR-GARCH volatility modeling

# 1. Fetch Data & Calculate Log Returns
df_raw <- tq_get("BTC-USD") %>%
  select(date, close) %>%
  filter(date >= last(date) - months(24)) %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  mutate(log_ret = log(close / lag(close))) %>%
  drop_na()

# 2. Add Lag Features on Log Returns
df_prepared <- df_raw %>%
  tk_augment_lags(log_ret, .lags = 1:20) %>%
  drop_na()

# 3. Time Series Split (10 Assessment Window)
split <- time_series_split(
  df_prepared,
  assess = 10,
  cumulative = TRUE
)

df_train <- training(split)
df_test  <- testing(split)

# 4. Recipe Setup (Predict Log Return, Not Level Price)
recipe_mlp <- recipe(log_ret ~ ., data = df_train) %>%
  step_rm(date, close) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

# modeltime::naive_reg() requires the date column as a predictor to parse the time index
recipe_naive <- recipe(log_ret ~ date, data = df_train)

# 5. Model Specifications
model_spec_mlp <- mlp(
  hidden_units = c(32, 16),
  epochs = 100,
  dropout = 0.05,
  learn_rate = 0.005
) %>%
  set_engine("brulee") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

model_spec_naive <- naive_reg() %>%
  set_engine("naive")

# 6. Workflow Construction & Model Fitting
workflow_mlp <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(recipe_mlp) %>%
  add_model(model_spec_mlp) %>%
  fit(df_train)

workflow_naive <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(recipe_naive) %>%
  add_model(model_spec_naive) %>%
  fit(df_train)

# 7. Predictions & Price Reconstruction (Reference Code Logic)
preds_mlp_ret   <- predict(workflow_mlp, df_test)
preds_naive_ret <- predict(workflow_naive, df_test)

df_results <- df_test %>%
  mutate(
    yesterday_close = lag(close, default = first(close)),
    actual      = close,
    pred_brulee = yesterday_close * exp(preds_mlp_ret$.pred),
    pred_naive  = yesterday_close * exp(preds_naive_ret$.pred)
  )

# ==============================================================================
# 7.5. GJR-GARCH (Skewed Student-t) Dynamic Volatility & Confidence Bands
# ==============================================================================
# Calculate MLP residuals on the training set
train_preds_mlp <- predict(workflow_mlp, df_train)$.pred
train_residuals <- df_train$log_ret - train_preds_mlp

# GJR-GARCH(1,1) specification with Skewed Student-t distribution for fat-tails and asymmetry
garch_spec <- ugarchspec(
  variance.model = list(model = "gjrGARCH", garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
  mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = FALSE),
  distribution.model = "sstd"
)

# Fit GJR-GARCH model on training residuals
garch_fit <- ugarchfit(spec = garch_spec, data = train_residuals, solver = "hybrid")

# Forecast conditional volatility for the 10-day test horizon
garch_fore <- ugarchforecast(garch_fit, n.ahead = 10)
dynamic_sigmas <- sigma(garch_fore) # 10-day dynamic conditional standard deviations

# Attach dynamic standard deviations to test results and compute dynamic confidence bounds
df_results <- df_results %>%
  mutate(
    conditional_sigma = as.vector(dynamic_sigmas),
    # Dynamically scaled confidence bounds in price space (± 1.96 * conditional_sigma)
    conf_hi = pred_brulee * exp(1.96 * conditional_sigma),
    conf_lo = pred_brulee * exp(-1.96 * conditional_sigma)
  )

# 8. Accuracy Table Construction (Yardstick on Original Price Scale)
accuracy_table <- tibble(
  .model_id   = c(1, 2),
  .model_desc = c("BRULEE MLP (32, 16) + GJR-GARCH", "NAIVE"),
  rmse        = c(rmse_vec(df_results$actual, df_results$pred_brulee),
                  rmse_vec(df_results$actual, df_results$pred_naive)),
  rsq         = c(rsq_vec(df_results$actual, df_results$pred_brulee),
                  rsq_vec(df_results$actual, df_results$pred_naive)),
  mape        = c(mape_vec(df_results$actual, df_results$pred_brulee),
                  mape_vec(df_results$actual, df_results$pred_naive)),
  mae         = c(mae_vec(df_results$actual, df_results$pred_brulee),
                  mae_vec(df_results$actual, df_results$pred_naive))
)

# Print Model Comparison Table
cat("=== MODEL ACCURACY EVALUATION TABLE (PRICE SCALE) ===\n")
cat(knitr::kable(accuracy_table, digits = 4, format = "simple"), sep = "\n")

# 9. Modern Interactive Plotly Visualization (Reference Style)
brulee_mape <- accuracy_table$mape[1]
df_eval <- df_results

# Custom Hover Text Data Frames
df_plot_actual <- df_eval %>% select(date, actual)  %>% mutate(text_actual = glue("<b>Actual Price:</b> {scales::dollar(actual, accuracy = 0.01)}<br><b>Date:</b> {format(date, '%b %d, %Y')}"))
df_plot_pred   <- df_eval %>% select(date, pred_brulee) %>% mutate(text_pred   = glue("<b>AI Prediction Price:</b> {scales::dollar(pred_brulee, accuracy = 0.01)}<br><b>Date:</b> {format(date, '%b %d, %Y')}"))
df_plot_hi     <- df_eval %>% select(date, conf_hi) %>% mutate(text_hi     = glue("<b>GJR-GARCH Upper Bound:</b> {scales::dollar(conf_hi, accuracy = 0.01)}<br><b>Date:</b> {format(date, '%b %d, %Y')}"))
df_plot_lo     <- df_eval %>% select(date, conf_lo) %>% mutate(text_lo     = glue("<b>GJR-GARCH Lower Bound:</b> {scales::dollar(conf_lo, accuracy = 0.01)}<br><b>Date:</b> {format(date, '%b %d, %Y')}"))

# Build Base GGPlot Layer
p <- ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = df_eval, aes(x = date, ymin = conf_lo, ymax = conf_hi), fill = "#808080", alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_point(data = df_plot_hi, aes(x = date, y = conf_hi, text = text_hi), color = "transparent", alpha = 0, size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = df_plot_lo, aes(x = date, y = conf_lo, text = text_lo), color = "transparent", alpha = 0, size = 3) +
  geom_line(data = df_plot_actual, aes(x = date, y = actual), color = "#2c3e50", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = df_plot_actual, aes(x = date, y = actual, text = text_actual), color = "#2c3e50", size = 2) +
  geom_line(data = df_plot_pred, aes(x = date, y = pred_brulee), color = "#e74c3c", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = df_plot_pred, aes(x = date, y = pred_brulee, text = text_pred), color = "#e74c3c", size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "", y = "",
    title = paste0(
      "<span style='color:#2c3e50'>BTC-USD Prices</span> vs ",
      "<span style='color:#e74c3c'>MLP + GJR-GARCH Dynamic Forecast</span><br>",
      "<span style='font-size:12px; color:#555555;'>10-Day Horizon | Out-of-Sample MAPE: ", round(brulee_mape, 2), "</span>"
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_markdown(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#ffffff", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#ffffff", color = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

# Typography Settings & Plotly Output
font_family <- list(family = "Roboto Slab, Sans-Serif", size = 16)
label_font  <- list(font = list(family = "Roboto Slab, Sans-Serif", size = 13))

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") %>%
  style(hoverlabel = label_font) %>%
  layout(font = font_family)

Conclusion

Combining machine learning with traditional econometrics produces a hybrid system that overcomes the limitations of both fields:

  1. Machine Learning captures non-linear relationships and trend movements.
  2. Econometrics (GARCH) supplies explicit statistical parameters for uncertainty and volatility clustering.

The resulting output provides realistic, dynamic risk envelopes that evolve with changing market regimes—giving quantitative traders and analysts a robust framework for volatility-aware decision-making.

items.author: rOpenSci

Mark Padgham is leaving rOpenSci at the end of October, and we want to take this moment to recognize his impact and say thank you for helping to shape rOpenSci.

items.content:
[This article was first published on rOpenSci - open tools for open science, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here)
Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

Mark Padgham is leaving rOpenSci at the end of October, and we want to take this moment to recognize his impact and say thank you for helping to shape rOpenSci.

Mark joined rOpenSci as a staff member in December 2019 to help us expand software peer review to statistical topics. However, Mark’s impact on rOpenSci has gone far beyond this one project. Mark has not only shaped how rOpenSci reviews statistical software, but has also built much of the tooling that supports the peer review processes, and R packages which not only support but also strengthen our community. If you have submitted a package to rOpenSci, reviewed or edited one, you have almost certainly used something Mark made!

Making a Mark

Mark’s most visible contribution is to statistical software peer review. Reviewing a package that implements statistical methods is a different job from reviewing a package that accesses an API. Mark tackled the task of translating what “good” means in a statistical package and how a reviewer can assess it. He recruited a new set of editors with the expertise to tackel this work and turned insights into a concrete set of statistical software standards and the guide that accompanies them (rOpenSci Statistical Software Testing and Peer Review Community Call). Mark also built the machinery to go with this new type review: pkgstats gathers information about a package’s structure, helps authors and editors see what a submission contains and how it is organised; srr allows package authors to document their adherence to statistical software standards.

The result of all this work was our first peer-reviewed statistical packages, published in November 2022, and to date we’ve had over 26 statistical packages go through this review! Anyone who has gone through statistical software review has benefited from the groundwork Mark laid.

The engine of software review

Peer review at rOpenSci is a human process, but it runs on a lot of automation, and a good part of that automation is Mark’s work.

Mark built and maintained pkgcheck, which runs automated checks on submitted packages, and the GitHub Action that allows anyone to run the same checks on their own repository. pkgcheck uses goodpractice, another package maintained by Mark, that recently rolled out a host of updates and extension. Mark maintained Buffy, the bot behind our chat review system on GitHub, which lets editors assign reviewers, track deadlines and move submissions along with simple comments, and many other pieces of infrastructure that make the whole system work.

Review is a human process

In early 2025, Mark became our new Software Review Lead. In this role he was in charge of editorial management, curating the current editorial board and planning its future. Mark helped guide peer-review through new challenges, such as how review should handle AI-assisted contributions, resulting in rOpenSci’s first AI policy; or how to deal with large software submissions, resulting in our first group peer review.

Tools for everyone

Mark’s care for rOpenSci goes beyond software. He researched alternatives to GitHub, sharing the results in Beyond GitHub, a thoughtful look at what it would mean for a community like ours to depend less on a single platform.

He has also served on our Code of Conduct committee, work that helps ensure rOpenSci remains a welcoming and safe community.

Mark also builds tools that help the wider R community. The allcontributors package, inspired by the allcontributors project, makes it easy to recognise everyone who contributes to a project, not just those who write code. His work on repometrics explores how to understand the health and activity of software repositories, and his work on deposits looks at how research data and software can be deposited in trusted repositories.

Thank you, Mark

Mark’s work has shaped how we review software, support contributors, and build a more reliable and sustainable open science ecosystem. Thank you, Mark, for building so much of the infrastructure and process that we rely on, and for leaving it in better shape than you found it.

If you have benefited from Mark’s work, reach out to Mark and let him know! You can keep following his work through his website and social media.
